hints: Think about what happens to the very ends of a linear chromosome each time DNA is copied before mitosis - is the copy always complete right to the tip?
If a little bit is lost from the tip each division, what would be at risk if important genes were right at the end, and how could a non-coding buffer help?
walkthrough:
Why chromosome ends are vulnerable**
Think of DNA replication. The machinery cannot copy right to the very tip of a linear chromosome, so a short piece is lost each cell cycle. Telomeres are repeated non-coding DNA at the ends that act as a disposable buffer.

Why that buffer matters**
By being shortened instead of coding DNA, telomeres maintain overall chromosome length. That allows cells to keep dividing and prevents loss or damage of genes, and stops the exposed ends being degraded or stuck together.
Final answer: Telomeres maintain chromosome length / prevent shortening. This permits continued replication and prevents loss of genes / protects ends from degradation.

hints: Compare the life history of a stem cell or cancer cell with a normal specialised cell - which ones need to go through the cell cycle and divide over and over again?
walkthrough:
Link telomerase to division**
Telomerase rebuilds telomeres. Most body cells divide only a few times, so they can afford to let telomeres shorten. Stem cells must keep producing new cells for life, and cancer cells divide continuously and without control, so both replicate their DNA again and again. Without extra telomerase their telomeres would quickly shorten and division would stop.
Final answer: Mitosis / cell cycle / DNA replication / cell division occurs continuously / regularly in both cell types, so telomeres must be rebuilt.

hints: Recall the two models for enzyme-substrate binding - one has a rigid active site that exactly matches, the other has a flexible active site that moulds around the substrate.
walkthrough:
Spot the flexible active site**
Lock and key means the active site is already a perfect rigid match. Here you are told the active site changes shape slightly to allow the enzyme-substrate complex to form. That moulding of the active site around the substrate is the induced fit theory.

hints: Read the two rates off Fig. 6.1 - find $0.2 \mu mol dm^{-3}$ on the steep rising part and $1.6 \mu mol dm^{-3}$ on the flat plateau, and estimate rate in arbitrary units for each.
Think in terms of active sites - at low substrate are most active sites empty or full, and at high substrate what becomes limiting when every active site is busy?
walkthrough:
Describe the difference from the graph**
At $0.2 \mu mol dm^{-3}$ the curve is still climbing steeply and rate is low, about 1.8-2.0 arbitrary units. At $1.6 \mu mol dm^{-3}$ the curve has levelled at Vmax, rate is high at 5.0 arbitrary units. So always quote both values with units to show the comparison.

Explain with active sites and complexes**
Rate depends on how often enzyme and substrate collide to form enzyme-substrate complexes. At low substrate, collisions are infrequent, many active sites are spare / unsaturated, so few complexes form per unit time and substrate concentration limits rate. At high substrate, collisions are frequent, all active sites are occupied / saturated, so maximum number of complexes form and adding more substrate cannot increase rate - enzyme concentration is now limiting.

Final answer: At $0.2 \mu mol dm^{-3}$ rate is low, about 2 arbitrary units; at $1.6 \mu mol dm^{-3}$ rate is high, maximum about 5 arbitrary units. At low concentration not all active sites are occupied / fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time, substrate is limiting. At high concentration all active sites are occupied / saturated / many more enzyme-substrate complexes form, enzyme concentration is limiting.
